tracks.title: Three parsers, three truths
tracks.text: Lesson 04 point 5 — the kernel. A deep dive, under org… the grammar. Three parsers, three truths. The parent lesson convinced you that org is parseable. Fair. But parseable is exactly where most systems begin to rot. [curious] A format earns a parser on the server… then a second one in the browser, so the page can render without a round trip… then a third, hand-rolled one in the CLI, because pulling the server in felt heavy. Three readers. Three languages. Three subtly different ideas of what a scheduled timestamp means. [sighs] And the rot isn't the parsers — it's that they drift. The server renders one thing… the client renders another… and now your format has no canonical meaning. Only a majority vote. So there's just one question worth asking. What actually reads my file… and is it the same thing everywhere? This lesson is the answer. And the answer is a single program.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The kernel is the one program that reads org for the whole ecosystem. A 552-line pure-function Rust crate. Two dependencies. Six verbs. And zero I/O. It takes a string… and it returns a string… and it is the same crate everywhere the grammar is read. There is no second copy. The whole contract is six functions, and every one of them is string to string. First… parse-headlines, which queries the tree. Second… tangle-plan, which compiles a build plan. Third… validate, which returns diagnostics. Fourth… check-upgrade, the safety gate. Fifth… render, which turns org into HTML. And sixth… lint, which is reserved — a stub today. The crate leans on just two libraries. One — serde, for the JSON it emits. And two — orgize, an MIT org-mode parser, for the heavy lifting of turning text into a tree. Everything the kernel adds… is opinion on top of that tree.

tracks.title: No host calls, no clock
tracks.text: No host calls… no clock. Every one of the six functions has the same shape. A borrowed string in. An owned string out. No function reads a file, opens a socket, asks the time, or calls back into a host. [curious] And that austerity isn't an aesthetic — it is the deployment mechanism. A function that touches no I/O has no opinion about where it runs. It needs no operating system, no event loop, no permissions… only a string, and a place to put the answer. So picture one source, fanning into three artifacts. In the middle… the crate itself — the six functions, written once. From it, three edges run out. The first edge compiles it with no features at all — a plain Rust library, to link into a binary. The second edge turns on the component feature, and produces a typed WebAssembly component. And the third edge turns on the browser feature, and produces a raw module a web page can instantiate. [excited] Here's the thing. The kernel is never ported to three surfaces. It is unchanged across them. As the crate's own source says it… there is no wasm version of the kernel logic.

tracks.title: Six verbs, one contract
tracks.text: Six verbs… one contract. The whole surface area is six functions, and each answers one question about an org document. Let me give you the ones that matter. Parse-headlines takes org and returns rows of JSON — it tells you what's in the tree. Tangle-plan takes org and returns a world — it tells you what the document builds into. Validate returns findings — is the plan sound, any dangling inputs. Render takes org and returns HTML. And every single one returns JSON or HTML… never a typed record. Because JSON is the type system at this boundary — the same on all three surfaces. Now, the honest part. [clears throat] Lint is a declared export that today returns a hardcoded empty array. It does nothing yet. The CLI's lint verb actually maps to validate — that's the function with the real diagnostics. The slot is reserved for style checks the kernel doesn't perform yet. And a lesson that told you otherwise… would be the first drift this whole design exists to prevent.

tracks.title: From headline to world
tracks.text: From headline… to world. Render and parse-headlines are the obvious verbs. Tangle-plan is the one that makes the kernel more than a parser. It reads a literate workflow — a tree of tagged headlines with source blocks — and computes a build plan shaped exactly like a WIT world. Imports, exports, components, and the edges between them. And none of that shape is written down by hand. It's derived. Picture the input. A headline called pipeline, tagged workflow, carrying a schedule property — six in the morning, every day. Under it, two children, each tagged component. The first… fetch — it uses the net capability, and it outputs raw. The second… summarize — it takes raw in, outputs report, and it's marked persist. Now run tangle. The kernel applies its rules in order. The workflow headline becomes the world, named pipeline. The schedule property wins as the cron string. Every uses becomes an import — so the import is net. Then the edges — the kernel matches one component's out to another's in. Fetch produces raw… summarize consumes raw… so one edge runs, fetch to summarize. And outputs nobody consumes become exports — so report is exported. [excited] Walk the result as a story. A capability called net flows in at the top. Data flows along the single raw edge, from fetch to summarize. And one output, report, leaves the world unconsumed, as its export. The recursion is the part that scales — a workflow nested under another becomes a sub-world. So an entire system of pipelines is one tree the kernel folds into one plan. A to-do list and a build system… turn out to be the same data structure. Tasks with dependencies. And the kernel refuses to make you learn it twice.

tracks.title: The upgrade gate
tracks.text: The upgrade gate. Once a world is live, changing it is dangerous — a redeploy can silently break the things downstream that depended on the old shape. Check-upgrade is the kernel's answer. Give it the old world and the new one, and it applies subtyping rules, and refuses anything breaking before it runs. The rules are short, and one-directional. First… remove a workflow, that's an error — something downstream may still call it. Second… remove an export, that's an error — a consumer of that output now breaks. Third… change a component's output type, that's an error — the old contract no longer holds. Fourth… add a new import, that's only a warning — a new capability is now required, so surface consent. And fifth… if nothing breaks, you get an empty array — a safe upgrade. The whole table in one line. Exports may grow but never shrink. Imports may shrink but never grow. And an output type may never change. [curious] Now watch it refuse a bad change, with nothing but stock wasmtime. Take a component called Build, that exported report as a string. And a new version, that now requires a network-email capability, and emits report as JSON instead. Invoke check-upgrade on the two. Back come three findings. One — the string export was removed… that's breaking. Two — a new email capability is now required… that's a warning, that becomes a consent prompt. And three — the component's output type changed… breaking too. Two errors. So the deploy… is refused.

tracks.title: Surface one — the CLI
tracks.text: Surface one — linked into the CLI. The first surface is the plainest. The kernel as an ordinary Rust library. The CLI crate — whose binary is named w-b-x — depends on it with default features off. No component glue, no wasi, no wrapper. With features off, the crate is just a library… and it links cleanly on native targets, and on the CLI's own wasm target too. Three verbs map straight through. w-b-x query calls parse-headlines. w-b-x tangle calls tangle-plan. And w-b-x lint calls validate — the real diagnostics, not the stub. A bare dash reads standard input, so org generated upstream never has to touch a temp file. And here's the point worth holding. These verbs run with no runtime server at all. The kernel is compiled into the binary in your hand. So you can query, tangle, and validate a file on a laptop… with nothing else installed.

tracks.title: Surface two — the runtime and desktop
tracks.text: Surface two — sealed in the runtime, and the desktop. This time you turn the same crate on the component feature, and run cargo component build. Out comes a typed WebAssembly component — four hundred and fourteen kilobytes — checked into git. A byte-identical copy lives in the desktop app. One artifact… two homes. In the runtime, a small process called Workbooks dot OQL embeds that wasm at compile time, instantiates it once, and calls the exports — with no hand-rolled pointer math, no manual memory bookkeeping, because the component model carries the types. Picture the exchange. A publish or web request asks that process to render some org. The process hands it to the one wasmtime instance. The instance returns HTML. And the page ships — its footer reading, rendered by the Workbooks OQL kernel. The same path drives more than rendering. The package manager calls tangle-plan to build a world. The socket dispatches parse, tangle, validate, and render. And publish renders a workbook to self-contained HTML, with no server required, because the kernel is embedded in the runtime. The desktop does the same trick natively — the wasm compiled right into the shell, and weave is just a call to render. Its tests prove a workbook weaves… with no Elixir, and no Docker. [curious] One honest nuance lives here. The world declares no imports — but the compiled artifact does import wasi, because Rust's standard library pulls it in. So the host starves it instead of trusting it. A blank wasi context. No preopens. Which means… no filesystem, ever. Render never touches a disk, because there is no disk to touch. And you don't need any Workbooks software to poke it — stock wasmtime, with an invoke flag, renders a headline straight from the command line.

tracks.title: Surface three — this very page
tracks.text: Surface three — this very page. The third surface drops the component model entirely, and builds raw wasm for the browser. Five hundred and thirty-seven kilobytes, with a deliberately tiny, hand-written boundary. Strings go in as a pointer and a length. Results come back as a single packed sixty-four-bit number — the high half is the pointer, the low half is the length. And all of the unsafe code in the entire crate lives in the forty-three lines of that one file. The component path has none. This build exports only four of the six functions, and it instantiates with zero imports. The whole client is about fifteen lines of JavaScript. Encode the string. Ask the module for memory. Write the bytes. Call the function. Unpack the number with two bit-shifts. And decode the result. That's it — no framework, no glue library. [excited] And it isn't a description. It's running right now, on this page. There's a box of org text, and beside it… that org rendered to HTML by the kernel, in your browser, with no server in the loop. The exact bytes the runtime ships, built for the web, instantiated right here. One honest note on weight — that convenience costs about five hundred and thirty-seven kilobytes. The component build is smaller, because its toolchain trims harder. Neither is tiny. Purity buys portability… not minimalism.

tracks.title: Where the story bends
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the story bends. The no-I/O, runs-anywhere story is true at the source level… and it bends in a few real places worth naming. First… the component imports wasi. The world declares no imports, but the binary pulls in wasi because Rust's standard library does — so the hosts starve it with a blank context and no preopens, rather than trusting it. Second… lint is a stub. It returns an empty array. The real diagnostics live in validate. Third… the upgrade gate isn't on every deploy yet. The rules exist and run, the runtime demonstrates them, but wiring it in front of every redeploy is ongoing work. Fourth… the browser build is five hundred and thirty-seven kilobytes. Real bytes, on a real page. Fifth… orgize does the parsing. The kernel is the opinionated lens — the tangle rules, the upgrade rules — not a parser written from scratch. And finally… a legacy fourth surface still lurks. The desktop carries an older vendored build from a dead monorepo. It predates the clean browser boundary, and it isn't the kernel this lesson teaches. [exhales] None of these break the core claim. One crate reads org for the whole ecosystem… and the places the purity story bends, are places the hosts contain — not places the meaning forks.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this the org-mode parser, rewritten? No. Orgize does the parsing. The kernel is the opinion on top — six functions of judgment. Why Rust, and not the Elixir host the runtime already has? Because the host can't run in a browser, or a standalone CLI. A pure Rust crate can compile to all three. The runtime is just one consumer. Can I call it myself? Yes — stock wasmtime invokes the component directly, and the browser build instantiates with zero imports in about fifteen lines of plain JavaScript. No SDK. Why six string-to-string functions, instead of typed records? One boundary everywhere. JSON is the type system, identical on every surface. And what happens if the kernel panics? [chuckles] A fault traps inside wasmtime. The instance is a sandbox — a panic becomes a trap the host catches, and it never reaches the runtime, the desktop shell, or the page. One last one. Does the kernel pass its own conformance check? No — and it's a lovely fact. The conformance test asks whether a component exports run. The kernel exports render, and tangle, instead. So the engine rejects it as a workbook. The reader the whole ecosystem is built on… isn't itself one of the things it reads.

tracks.title: Back up to org
tracks.text: So that's the kernel. Not three parsers that drift… one pure crate, string in, string out, the same everywhere the grammar is read. Linked into the CLI. Sealed in the runtime and the desktop. And built raw for the browser — the very bytes that rendered the demo on this page. [curious] The way back up is short. This is a deep dive under org — lesson four — the grammar this machine reads. Go back there for the syntax itself. And if you want to follow what the kernel computes — tangling, for how a document becomes a build plan… and workflows, for the plans it compiles and renders. The kernel is the one reader. Everything else… is what it reads.
